ANOVA with several factors

  • Each with two or more levels
  • Assume two factors: A with \(i=1,2,...a\) levels, and B with \(j=1,2,...,b\) levels
  • If all levels of A are tested with all levels of B we have a complete crossed design.
  • Assume there are \(k=1,2,...,n\) replicates of all \(ab\) level combinations.

Illustration of two-factor case

https://solve.shinyapps.io/Factorialdemo/

The Model

Model: \[y_{ijk} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + \alpha\beta_{ij} + \epsilon_{ijk}\]

where \(\epsilon_{ijk} \sim N(0,\sigma^2)\).

Parametrization (restrictions)

  • Sum-to-zero: \(\sum_i {\alpha}_i =0\), \(\sum_j {\beta}_j=0\), \(\sum_i \alpha\beta_{ij}=0\) and \(\sum_j \alpha\beta_{ij}=0\).

  • Reference levels: \(\alpha_1 = 0\), \(\beta_1 = 0\), \(\alpha\beta_{1,j}=0\) for all \(j\) and \(\alpha\beta_{i,1}=0\) for all \(i\).

Example: Animal diets - The “growth data”

R analysis

For reference level analysis, see “the R-book” on page 517.

Let’s again use the sum-to-zero parametrization here:

mod2 <- lm(gain ~ diet + supplement + diet:supplement, 
           data=weights, contrasts = "contr.sum")
## Warning in model.matrix.default(mt, mf, contrasts): non-list contrasts argument
## ignored

Equivalent model calls in R:

  • gain ~ diet + supplement + diet:supplement
  • gain ~ diet*supplement
  • gain ~ (diet + supplement)^2

Interaction plots

Means of diet:supplement combinations.

library(effects)
plot(allEffects(mod2,confidence.level=.99),layout=c(3,1), 
     rotx=90,alternating=FALSE)

Model parameter estimation

For balanced data the least squares estimators for the model parameters are (sum-to-zero):

\(\widehat{\mu} = \bar{y}_{...}\)

\(\widehat{\alpha}_i = \bar{y}_{i..}-\bar{y}_{...}\)

\(\widehat{\beta}_j = \bar{y}_{.j.}-\bar{y}_{...}\)

\(\widehat{\alpha\beta}_{ij} = \bar{y}_{ij.} - \bar{y}_{i..} - \bar{y}_{.j.} + \bar{y}_{...}\)

And as usual, the noise variance estimate is:

\(\widehat{\sigma}^2 = MSE\)

Summary with estimates of effects:

We want to test hypotheses

Interaction effects? \[H_0:\alpha\beta_{11} = \alpha\beta_{12} = \cdots = \alpha\beta_{ab} = 0\]

Main effect of A? \[H_0:\alpha_1 = \alpha_2=\cdots=\alpha_a = 0\]

Main effect of B? \[H_0:\beta_1 = \beta_2 = \cdots = \beta_b = 0\]

Splitting of sums of squares

The Total Sums of Squares measures total variability: \[SST = \sum_i \sum_j \sum_k (y_{ijk} - \bar{y}_{...})^2\]

Can be split into: \[SST = SSA + SSB + SSAB + SSE\]

Degrees of freedom follow correspondingly as \[(N-1) = [(a-1)] + [(b-1)] + [(a-1)(b-1)] + [ab(n-1)]\]

F-tests

Interaction: Reject \(H_0\) if \[F = \frac{MSAB}{MSE} = \frac{SSAB/(a-1)(b-1)}{SSE/ab(n-1)}\] is larger than \(F_{\alpha,(a-1)(b-1),ab(n-1)}\) or p-value < \(\alpha\).

Main effect A: Reject \(H_0\) if \[F = \frac{MSA}{MSE} > F_{\alpha,(a-1),ab(n-1)}\]

Main effect B: Reject \(H_0\) if \[F = \frac{MSB}{MSE} > F_{\alpha,(b-1),ab(n-1)}\]

Note: The complete crossed design gives “orthogonal effects”. The SS’s are independent, and, apart from SSE, they do not change when effects are removed/added to the model.

Analysis of covariance - ANCOVA

The dataset birth in the BIAS.data package holds records of 189 birth weights from Massachusetts, USA, and some additional variables. Three of the variables are,

Var Description
LWT Weight of mother.
SMK YES if mother smokes and NO otherwise.
BWT Birth weight (RESPONSE).

The main question is: Does mother’s smoking affect birth weight and does it depend on the mother weight?

We have both a categorical and a continuous predictor for the response variable.

The data

##   LWT SMK  BWT
## 1 120 YES  709
## 2 130  NO 1021
## 3 187 YES 1135
## 4 105  NO 1330
## 5  85  NO 1474
## 6 150  NO 1588
## 7  97  NO 1588

Scatterplot with separate linear models for smokers and non-smokers

## Warning in applyDefaults(regLine, defaults = list(method = lm, lty = 1, :
## unnamed arguments, will be ignored

ANCOVA as regression with indicator variable

Let \(y = BWT\) and \(x_1 = LWT\) and define \[ x_2 = \left\{ \begin{array}[cc] \ 0 & \mbox{if smoker}\\ 1 & \mbox{if non-smoker} \end{array} \right. \]

Assume the model \[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 x_{2i} + \epsilon_i \] where \(\epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\).

Fitting the model in R

birth4 <- lm(BWT ~ LWT + SMK, data=birth, contrasts = "contr.treatment")
birth4
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = BWT ~ LWT + SMK, data = birth, contrasts = "contr.treatment")
## 
## Coefficients:
## (Intercept)          LWT     SMK(YES)  
##    2500.174        4.238     -270.013

Explain coefficients

The estimated model(s)

The model with interaction term

Assume that we expand the model with an interaction term between LWT and SMK \[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 x_{2i} + \beta_3 x_{1i}\cdot x_{2i} + \epsilon_i \] with \(\epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\).

Lets see how the model is for different values of \(x_{2i}\)

  • Are model assumptions met?
  • Are there significant effects of LWT and/or SMK?
  • How is the model fit in terms of \(R^2\)? Critizise the model!
